top_evidence.document_title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: Background The Mediterranean diet has been associated with improved metabolic health among adults. This meta-­ analysis aimed to evaluate the association between adherence to a Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome among children and adolescents. Methods A systematic review of the literature was conducted by searching PubMed, the Excerpta Medica Database (Embase, via OvidSP), Scopus and Web of Science, covering publications from inception to April 2024. Studies were included if they evaluated the association between adherence to a Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome among children and adolescents. A random-­ effects model was used to estimate the summary effect size. Results A total of eight studies involving children and adolescents aged 6 to 19 years were included in the meta-­ analysis (n=6562, 50% girls). Low adherence to the Mediterranean diet was associated with greater odds of metabolic syndrome than was medium/high adherence (odds ratio [OR] = 2.18, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.45 to 3.28; p < 0.001; inconsistency index [ I 2 ] = 64.15%). Conclusion This meta-­ analysis suggested that increased adherence to a Mediterranean diet is associated with lower probabilities of having cardiometabolic risk among children and adolescents. Thus, our findings suggest that public health strategies are needed to implement and promote effective actions toward healthy eating habits in children and adolescents.

top_evidence.document_title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: To be eligible for inclusion in the present review, studies needed to meet the following criteria: (i) were children or adolescents aged 5-19 years, all countries and ethnic backgrounds; (ii) had a MetS outcome; (iii) had an adherence to the MedDiet assessed by a validated questionnaire; and (iv) had a longitudinal and cross-­ sectional study design. However, to narrow the scope of the meta-­ analysis, only studies that associated the MedDiet with the outcome of MetS were included. In contrast, the exclusion criteria included adults and adolescents/children with evidence of metabolic or autoimmune liver disease, diabetes or the presence of known systemic disease. Studies were also excluded if they presented duplicate data from the same source and year. When two studies used duplicate data from the same source and year, the study with the larger sample size was selected.

top_evidence.text: A search strategy was used to identify all eligible studies published before 22 April 2024. The search strategy included controlled vocabulary terms specific to each database along with keywords derived from scoping index articles relevant to this meta-­ analysis. The following terms related to the MedDiet were used: MEDdiet, Mediterranean Diet Quality Index for Children and Adolescents (KIDMED) score, MedDiet score, MedDiet and hypertension, MedDiet and diabetes, KIDMED and MedDiet score. The following outcome terms related to MetS were included: MetS or components (hyperlipidaemia, hypertriglyceridaemia, insulin resistance, hyperglycaemia, hypertension) combined with health. top_evidence.document_title: Association between adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome in children and adolescents: a systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: To be eligible for inclusion in the present review, studies needed to meet the following criteria: (i) were children or adolescents aged 5-19 years, all countries and ethnic backgrounds; (ii) had a MetS outcome; (iii) had an adherence to the MedDiet assessed by a validated questionnaire; and (iv) had a longitudinal and cross-­ sectional study design. However, to narrow the scope of the meta-­ analysis, only studies that associated the MedDiet with the outcome of MetS were included. In contrast, the exclusion criteria included adults and adolescents/children with evidence of metabolic or autoimmune liver disease, diabetes or the presence of known systemic disease. Studies were also excluded if they presented duplicate data from the same source and year. When two studies used duplicate data from the same source and year, the study with the larger sample size was selected.

top_evidence.text: A total of eight cross-­ sectional studies were included in the meta-­ analysis. We identified 3775 articles by searching the databases MEDLINE (via PubMed), Embase (Ovid) and Web of Science. A total of 1456 studies were excluded because of duplication, while 1565 were classified as ineligible by automation tools. Another 546 studies were removed for additional reasons. We examined the titles and abstracts of 208 studies and excluded 157 on the basis of our findings. We screened 51 articles for eligibility. Eight studies were included in the meta-­ analysis. elements.quote: Limitations of the present systematic review include the fact that the degree of adherence to the MedDiet could be subject to regional variations, potentially introducing further biases. elements.quote: These findings are consistent with previous research in adults, suggesting that adherence to the MedDiet may have favourable effects on MetS outcomes. 17 However, unlike the study performed by Bakaloudi et al , 17 our study focused only on children and adolescents, presenting a well-­ designed systematic review and meta-­ analysis of paediatric populations.
elements.reason: The discussion explicitly situates the study's results relative to prior research (noting consistency with adult studies and contrasting with Bakaloudi et al), and further explains potential mechanisms and public-health implications, thereby interpreting the results in the context of other evidence.

elements.quote: Limitations of the present systematic review include the fact that the degree of adherence to the MedDiet could be subject to regional variations, potentially introducing further biases. For example, individuals with high adherence to the MedDiet living in Mediterranean areas may consume certain foods more frequently than may those residing in non-­ Mediterranean regions. Furthermore, the need to convert data for the purpose of quantitative analysis presents an additional limitation to our study; additionally, we restricted our inclusion criteria to studies published in English. In addition, most of the included studies were cross-­ sectional, which limits the ability to establish causality or determine the temporal relationship between adherence to the MedDiet and MetS outcomes. However, further well-­ designed prospective cohort studies and randomised controlled trials are needed to confirm the findings of our meta-­ analysis and elucidate the underlying mechanisms involved. All the studies used a cross-­ sectional design, so the observed results should be interpreted with caution. Another significant limitation is that studies use different questionnaires to determine adherence to the MedDiet, as well as different points for comparisons between categories. Additionally, there is no single criterion for defining MetS in the paediatric population, so the observed inconsistency could be due to these limitations. Finally, a formal assessment of the certainty of evidence (eg, using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach) was not performed, as this was beyond the scope of the present review.
elements.reason: The Discussion explicitly lists multiple limitations of the included evidence: regional variation in adherence measurement, data conversion, English-only inclusion, predominance of cross-sectional designs limiting causality, heterogeneous questionnaires and MetS definitions, and absence of a formal certainty assessment.

elements.quote: Limitations of the present systematic review include the fact that the degree of adherence to the MedDiet could be subject to regional variations, potentially introducing further biases. For example, individuals with high adherence to the MedDiet living in Mediterranean areas may consume certain foods more frequently than may those residing in non-­ Mediterranean regions. Furthermore, the need to convert data for the purpose of quantitative analysis presents an additional limitation to our study; additionally, we restricted our inclusion criteria to studies published in English. In addition, most of the included studies were cross-­ sectional, which limits the ability to establish causality or determine the temporal relationship between adherence to the MedDiet and MetS outcomes. However, further well-­ designed prospective cohort studies and randomised controlled trials are needed to confirm the findings of our meta-­ analysis and elucidate the underlying mechanisms involved. All the studies used a cross-­ sectional design, so the observed results should be interpreted with caution. Another significant limitation is that studies use different questionnaires to determine adherence to the MedDiet, as well as different points for comparisons between categories. Additionally, there is no single criterion for defining MetS in the paediatric population, so the observed inconsistency could be due to these limitations. Finally, a formal assessment of the certainty of evidence (eg, using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach) was not performed, as this was beyond the scope of the present review.
